claim_counting: 288 claims across 5 genres: tagline, place, date_range, description, debatable, each listen_for (3), each hallmark (5), each link's label and reason (2 per link; 5, 5, 6, 6 and 12 links), each artist's dates, summary, 2 contributions, recording and study prompt (6 per artist; 4, 4, 5, 5, 5 artists), and each of the 3 landmark recordings. reacted_against counted for indie-rock and post-punk (both supported); null for the other three. Seven 'unsupported' items are citation-only: the fact is true in an uncited section of the same article (Sinatra/Dorsey, Page/Oklahoma, Houston/Newark, Spears/Mississippi, Siouxsie 2002, PiL 1992, plus the indie debatable).
study_prompts: All 23 prompts were checked by machine: each is exactly the fixed opening + the artist's summary and contributions word for word + the 'Start with <recording> (<year>)' close, so none goes beyond the card. They inherit the card's errors, so regenerate after fixes for Irving Berlin (recording), Bing Crosby (year 1942), Michael Jackson (c2), Whitney Houston (summary), Bikini Kill (c2 and the year-less recording) and Siouxsie and the Banshees (c1).

content_rules.own_recording: 22 of 23 artist recordings are credited to the artist and named in their own article. Exception: Irving Berlin's 'Alexander's Ragtime Band' is his composition; no 1911 recording by him is in the corpus.
content_rules.rankings: Cards avoid the source's 'best-selling of all time', 'greatest', Rolling Stone and Guinness ranks throughout (Thriller, Madonna, Houston, Spears, BTS, Blackpink, Slanted and Enchanted, Entertainment!, Is This It). One residual chart superlative: Houston c2 'a record at the time'.
content_rules.hedges: Kept well: Michael Jackson allegations (accused 1993, settled 1994, acquitted 2005 on other charges, 2019 documentary 'made further allegations'), 'considered the first K-pop idol group', 'one of the first idol boy bands', 'probably mocks', 'is described as highly influential', 'often called the Queen of K-pop'. Dropped: 'partly shaped' (pop hallmark5), 'generally predates' (trad-pop description), 'less completely' (trad-pop hallmark3).
content_rules.link_reasons: All 34 link reasons are plain statements about the music, with no judgement words; failing ones are listed above for drift only.

items.claim: ...came before rock and roll took over in the mid-1950s... In the swing era and after, crooners carried these songs to the top of the charts.
cited: Traditional_pop#Mid-1940s to mid-1950s: height of popularity
items.note: Source hedges 'generally predates'; nothing cited says crooners took the songs 'to the top of the charts' (the section says the swing era 'made stars of' singers).

fix.text: Traditional pop is the Western popular music that generally came before rock and roll and pop in the mid-1950s. Its songs were written by Broadway, Tin Pan Alley and Hollywood songwriters, and many became 'standards': songs so widely known that many artists recorded them. The swing era made stars of singers such as Bing Crosby, Frank Sinatra and Patti Page.

items.claim: Tin Pan Alley began around 1885, when music publishers crowded into one Manhattan district, later West 28th Street.
items.note: Source says the name 'originally' referred to West 28th Street; 'later' reverses it.

fix.text: Tin Pan Alley is usually dated from about 1885, when music publishers set up shop in one Manhattan district, originally a stretch of West 28th Street. Families bought sheet music to play new songs at home, and 'song pluggers' at the piano demonstrated new tunes to push sales. The name probably mocks the din of many cheap pianos playing at once, and Irving Berlin was among the writers who frequented it.

sources.section: New York City before Tin Pan Alley

items.claim: ...in the 1910s and 1920s jazz and blues styles. Sources note a strong African American influence from ragtime, blues and jazz.
items.note: 'strong' is not in the source (it says 'a vernacular African-American impact'), and the source's hedge that jazz and blues were taken up 'less completely' is dropped. 'Cakewalk' is unglossed.

fix.text: Tin Pan Alley started with melodramatic ballads and comic novelty songs, then took up the cakewalk (a strutting dance rhythm) and ragtime, and in the 1910s and 1920s published songs in the new jazz and blues styles, though less completely, since its songs had to suit amateur singers. Writers note an African American influence from ragtime, the blues and jazz. Berlin's 'Alexander's Ragtime Band' (1911) revived the ragtime craze.

fix.text: K-pop grew in South Korea in the 1990s as a youth subculture, with Korean musicians drawing on Western dance music, hip-hop, R&B and rock. items.claim: ...krautrock... Its lighter, poppier cousin, new wave, took the same post-punk moment to the charts and, through MTV, to America.
items.note: New wave emerged in the mid-to-late 1970s alongside punk (the terms were first used interchangeably), so it didn't take 'the same post-punk moment' anywhere. 'Krautrock' and 'dub' are unglossed.

fix.text: Post-punk grew in the late 1970s, mainly in Britain, as bands kept punk's do-it-yourself energy but dropped its raw simplicity for a more experimental approach. They borrowed from dub (reggae remixed with heavy echo and bass), funk, disco, krautrock (experimental German rock), electronics and avant-garde art, and from writers such as J. G. Ballard and William S. Burroughs. Its lighter, more pop-oriented relative, new wave, grew up alongside it, reached the charts from 1979 and, through MTV, spread across America.

fix.text: Producers such as Martin Hannett, Steve Lillywhite and Dennis Bovell devised unorthodox studio techniques. Hannett gave Joy Division an eerie sense of space, with Peter Hook's bass carrying the melody and the guitar leaving gaps, on records for Manchester's independent Factory label.

fix.text: New wave took a lighter, more melodic route, with hooks, quirky humour and synths. Sire Records' Seymour Stein pushed the name to sell his acts from CBGB, the New York punk club; Blondie, from the same scene, had 'Heart of Glass', the first new wave single to reach number one in the US, and MTV spread new wave across America from 1981.
